content:
Earlier this year, I replaced my battery-powered push mower with a robot mower that can be controlled via iPhone. You can manually drive it along the border of your yard to build a virtual map. Once everything is set up, it automatically takes over the mowing according to a preset schedule.

Earlier, I also tried another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I believe it may be an easier choice for many people.

Camera-driven automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how the two machines understand your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the border with my iPhone to create an initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses a system the company calls TerraVision 2.0. Three cameras let the mower automatically map the lawn and navigate without buried boundary wires or a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic method for creating the initial map did take longer. However, for people who are less fond of tinkering with technology, this approach is likely easier to get started with.

To test this idea, I had my mom, who lives in another state, set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She replied that everything worked well. That said, it's harder for me to know whether she'd have the patience to first manually drive the robot around the entire border and then manually mark the areas to avoid.

The automatic mapping did create one small quirk in my front yard. There's no fence or other physical separation between my lawn and my neighbour's, so the TerraMow initially included part of the neighbour's lawn in my map.

I fixed the problem afterwards by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. That said, if your lawn doesn't have clear visual boundaries, you may need to pay special attention during the initial mapping process.

Watching through the mower's cameras

The cameras on the TerraMow also enable one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used the iPhone Mirroring feature on my Mac to keep this feed open in a large window. I could work indoors while watching the mower move around the backyard from its own perspective.

This feature isn't essential for automated mowing, but it makes the robot more engaging, and it occasionally explains why it slows down or avoids something. The Anthbot M9 doesn't have a comparable camera view.

The two iPhone apps share a lot in common otherwise. Both let you schedule work times, adjust mowing behaviour, create zones, mark areas to avoid, and remote-control the mower.

TerraMow has one particularly nice design touch for that last feature. In addition to the traditional left/right virtual controls, its app also offers a one-handed joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and guide the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run on a preset schedule without any intervention. Still, TerraMow's joystick control is a genuine joy to use for tidying up missed spots.

Sometimes I almost feel as if I'm controlling the robot with my mind (and that feeling is great). I can hold the iPhone down by my side, give it subtle thumb movements to walk, and the mower follows my instructions.

Every robot mower app should copy this control design.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 also mows more aggressively than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was also noticeably louder while working.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow noisy. But the difference between the two is clear. The Anthbot can run so quietly that it's easy to forget it's still there, including when it's mowing after sunset with its headlight on.

Because TerraMow relies on cameras to navigate, it needs daylight to operate reliably. Daytime scheduling is therefore even more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and well built. It's also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage that covers the charging dock, whereas Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has performed reliably. I relied on it for several weeks in a row without needing to do any routine mowing myself.

When adaptive mapping gets too clever

The visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can occasionally work against it.

The mower continually adjusts the map based on what it sees. After each session, saving these changes takes some time, during which you temporarily can't do anything else in the app.

After a few days of rain, I ran into an interesting edge case. Some puddles appeared in parts of the yard, and TerraMow sensibly avoided that area on its next run.

The grass inside the skipped circular patch then grew taller. Over time, the mower seemed to treat that growth as something to keep avoiding, so even after the ground dried out, that patch of grass was consistently ignored.

I manually mowed that taller patch using the app's remote control, and that fixed the problem. Once the grass recovered, automated mowing resumed working normally there.

Regular edging can also help TerraMow reach the boundaries with more confidence. Tall grass along unclear borders might otherwise be mistaken for an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on the boundaries and obstacles I set myself. This method requires more work up front, but it also avoids the map changing its mind and refusing to mow a patch of grass.

9to5Mac's take

After using both systems, for most people I lean toward TerraMow's camera-based approach.

Burying boundary wires is a complete non-starter for me, and installing an RTK base station is one more piece of hardware that has to be placed, powered, and maintained. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless. The initial mapping took longer, an invisible property line needed manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook overgrown grass for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are still manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 delivers simpler setup, reliable automated mowing, an engaging live camera feed, and the best manual controls I've seen in any robot mower app.

I genuinely enjoy yard work, but mowing is the most repetitive part of it. Handing that off to a robot gives me more time for landscaping, edging, and detail work, while the lawn still stays tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 does this well enough that I can recommend it, especially for people who want a robot mower but don't want to bury wires, install an RTK antenna, or manually drive an iPhone around the entire yard.

Amazon is currently offering the TerraMow V1000 with a promo code, bringing the price down to $999 after applying a $200 code on the site. You can also buy it from TerraMow's official website.
